title: Time-Series Anomaly Detection
shortDefinition: The identification of unusual patterns in sequential data over time — critical for monitoring AI, IoT, and operations.
definition: Time-series anomaly detection identifies data points or patterns in sequential, time-ordered data that deviate significantly from expected historical behavior — flagging sudden spikes, unexpected drops, seasonal pattern violations, or gradual drifts that indicate something has changed and warrants investigation. The time dimension adds meaningful complexity to anomaly detection: what's 'normal' often depends on time of day, day of week, or seasonal trends, meaning a value that's anomalous on a Tuesday morning might be perfectly normal on a Friday afternoon.

sections.title: How time-series anomaly detection differs from standard anomaly detection
sections.description: Time-series anomaly detection specifically models temporal structure — time-of-day, seasonal cycles, and trends — before flagging deviations.

content.text: General anomaly detection identifies unusual individual data points or records without considering their position in a time sequence. Time-series anomaly detection specifically models the temporal structure of data — learning what 'normal' looks like across time of day, day of week, seasonal cycles, and trend directions — before flagging deviations from those learned temporal patterns. This temporal context is essential for meaningful anomaly detection in monitoring use cases: a server response time of 500ms is anomalous at 3am (when traffic is low) but normal at 2pm (peak traffic), and only time-aware models can make this distinction.

items: Standard anomaly detection — ignores time sequence.
Time-series anomaly detection — models temporal structure.
Time-of-day context — same value can be normal or anomalous depending on time.
Seasonal patterns — learns recurring cycles to avoid false alarms.
Temporal context — essential for meaningful monitoring.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: A value that's anomalous on a Tuesday morning might be perfectly normal on a Friday afternoon — time-series anomaly detection understands this temporal context.

Time-series anomaly detection serves several high-value monitoring use cases: infrastructure monitoring (detecting unusual patterns in server metrics, API latency, or error rates that indicate system problems before user impact); AI model performance monitoring (detecting drift or accuracy degradation in deployed models' prediction distributions over time — see: Model Drift); IoT and sensor monitoring (flagging equipment behavior that deviates from normal operating patterns, enabling predictive maintenance); business metric surveillance (detecting unexpected changes in revenue, conversion, or operational KPIs that warrant investigation); and security anomaly detection (identifying unusual access patterns, transaction volumes, or behavioral sequences that indicate potential compromise).

sections.title: Limitations and risks of time-series anomaly detection

content.text: Time-series anomaly detection has limitations. It requires sufficient historical data to model temporal patterns accurately. Seasonal and trend patterns can change, requiring model updates. False alarm rates can be high without careful tuning. The approach may miss anomalies that don't manifest as statistical deviations from historical patterns. Rare event detection is challenging. External factors (promotions, outages, market events) can create patterns that look anomalous but are explainable by context not captured in the data. Alert fatigue remains a risk without thoughtful severity routing.

items: Data requirements — needs sufficient historical data.
Pattern change — seasonal patterns can evolve over time.
False alarm risk — high without careful tuning.
Context gaps — may flag explainable events as anomalies.
Rare event challenge — infrequent anomalies are hard to model.
Alert fatigue — needs thoughtful severity routing to avoid overload.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about time-series anomaly detection

items.question: What's the difference between time-series anomaly detection and time-series forecasting?
items.answer: Forecasting predicts future values; anomaly detection flags past or current values that deviate from what was expected — they're complementary, and anomaly detection systems often use forecasting models internally to generate the expected-value baseline they compare against.

items.question: Can time-series anomaly detection catch gradual drifts, not just sudden spikes?
items.answer: Yes — drift detection specifically identifies gradual trend changes that individually look small but cumulatively represent significant deviation from historical baseline.

items.question: How much historical data is needed to train a time-series anomaly detection model?
items.answer: Enough to observe representative seasonal and trend patterns — typically at minimum several months, with more history enabling more reliable modeling of annual seasonality.

items.question: Is time-series anomaly detection supervised or unsupervised?
items.answer: Both approaches exist — unsupervised (learning normal patterns without labeled anomaly examples) is more common since labeled historical anomaly examples are often scarce; supervised approaches are used when labeled examples are available and reliability is critical.

items.question: How long does building a time-series anomaly detection system take?
items.answer: 10–30 weeks depending on metric stream count and alert routing complexity.

items.question: Can time-series anomaly detection be applied to AI model monitoring?
items.answer: Yes — monitoring deployed model prediction distributions for drift over time is a standard time-series anomaly detection application in MLOps.

items.question: What is the difference between point anomalies and collective anomalies in time series?
items.answer: Point anomalies are individual data points that deviate from expected values (e.g., a sudden spike). Collective anomalies are sequences of points that deviate together, even if individually they might not be anomalous (e.g., a sustained but gradual change). Time-series anomaly detection handles both.

items.question: Can time-series anomaly detection handle multiple seasonalities?
items.answer: Yes — modern systems can model daily, weekly, and yearly seasonalities simultaneously. ClickMasters builds models that capture the specific seasonality patterns in your data.

items.question: What are common algorithms for time-series anomaly detection?
items.answer: Common approaches include statistical methods (ARIMA, seasonal decomposition), machine learning methods (Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM), and deep learning (LSTM autoencoders). ClickMasters selects the right approach based on your data characteristics and requirements.

items.question: How do you handle holidays and special events in time-series anomaly detection?
items.answer: Holidays and special events can be treated as known exogenous factors or as patterns to be learned. ClickMasters incorporates holiday calendars and event data to prevent normal special-day patterns from being flagged as anomalies.
